content:
MS NOW hosts on Tuesday night discussed the potential ramifications of Democrats sweeping statewide contests in Texas, with Rachel Maddow noting shifts after the 2030 U.S. census could cement the national political landscape as “a totally different ballgame.”

Maddow was extrapolating on the historic victories in the Lone Star State with a panel of fellow hosts after Democrat James Talarico beat GOP opponent Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat and Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R).

“And the way population shifts are happening in this country right now, Texas is likely to get a big boost in terms of the number of congressional districts it has — and a big boost in the number of electoral votes that it has after the 2030 census,” Maddow said Tuesday.

She continued, “And if the Democratic Party is winning statewide in Texas now, what we thought of as the Electoral College … landscape, if Texas moves in the Electoral College, the whole country is a different landscape. National politics is a totally different ballgame.”

Maddow added how “exciting” it was to see Talarico beat Paxton, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump despite a litany of past scandals and a mugshot, but said the young, “appealing seminarian-type centrist” was arguably “crafted from birth” to do so.

“I would have been talking about 2030 and the Electoral College as something that was going to be a very different scenario for Democrats ever having the chance of winning the presidency again,” said Maddow, prompting her fellow MS NOW hosts to chime in.

“I just want to say one other thing about Texas and about the general thing that you just said,” teased Chris Hayes. “There’s a lot of implications. One of them is, I was really upset by the grossness and the cruelty of the closing message of Republicans in Michigan, about the things they said about Abdul El-Sayed, but also the attack on trans folks that has just become so toxic and so common and so cruel and so ceaseless. And it was every ad. ... You watch a Sunday football game, and it was, ‘These people are the reason. This is the problem.’”

Trump had made the midterms all about himself despite disastrous approval ratings, told voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot and lobbed racist attacks against Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who ultimately won his Senate race — only for the blue wave Tuesday to serve as a referendum.

“And to see the repudiation of that approach … that people are like, ‘I don’t care about that’ and ‘I reject that,’ and that there’s some salvaging of decency for people that are our neighbors and our friends and our loved ones. … I’m just very, very grateful,” Hayes said Tuesday.

MS NOW host Nicolle Wallace took things further and argued this massive “repudiation” of Trump is actually a “revolt” — which started when everyday people in Minneapolis and Chicago who were “way ahead of politicians” took to the streets to risk their lives in protest.

“Bruce Springsteen and Tom Morello followed, but this is a completely citizen-driven revolt,” Wallace said Tuesday. “And whenever we’ve used ‘repudiation,’ ‘rebuke’ — this is now a revolt. … This is just the American people saying, ‘This is not at all what I wanted.’”
